caption:
Roughly 73% of Indian workers now use AI tools regularly. Forbes India made the point this week: AI skill alone doesn't make a leader.

For years, your edge was preparation. You read the deck twice. You knew the numbers cold. You were the most analysed person in the room.

That moat is gone. Everyone walks in with the same analysis now.

What remains is how you hold the room while you deliver it. Bearing. Tone. The pause before you answer, held long enough that people lean in instead of talking over you.

In 35 years of command, Colonel Suhag watched officers with identical briefings get completely different results. The difference was never the information. It was the man delivering it.

The data is commodity. Command is not.

topic.title: AI fluency is table stakes; presence is the tiebreaker
topic.angle: With roughly 73% of Indian workers using AI tools regularly, analysis is no longer a moat — destabilising news for a manager who has always competed on being the most prepared person in the room.
topic.why_now: Forbes India published a piece four days ago arguing India needs AI and business skills together, putting this conversation actively in Indian business media this week.
